title: Slabless batcher exploration journal
content:
Objective:
- Run a targeted set of experiments to understand the tradeoffs of a slabless continuous batcher (no fixed per-slab reservation) vs current slabbed allocator. Focus on tail latency (p95/p99), fairness across tenants, and GPU utilization under mixed traffic patterns.

Background / motivation:
- Current allocator uses fixed-size slabs (micro-shards) for requests which simplifies isolation but introduces fragmentation and sometimes long waits for slab fill under bursty small requests.
- The slabless variant attempts to form batches greedily across slots with soft isolation signals (priority tags + age weights) to reduce head-of-line delays and improve average latency. We suspect improvements at low QPS but possible regressions on fairness and worst-case p99.

High-level hypotheses:
1) Slabless reduces p50/p95 in interspersed small-request workloads (chatty token-by-token style) by 10-30% by avoiding wasted reserved capacity.
2) Under heavy mixed QPS (warm heavy tenants + many small tenants), slabless may increase p99 by introducing priority inversion unless we attach age or jitter admission control.
3) Slabless will modestly increase GPU occupancy variance (more bursty kernels) which can marginally increase per-token cost but improve end-user latency for many requests.

Testbed and instrumentation:
- Cluster: 8x A10 nodes (single-GPU perf nodes) and 4x A100 nodes for stress tests.
- Serving binary: runner/v1.19-sl3 (branch: slabless-explore).
- Tools: nsys traces, perf, eBPF task wake traces (bcc), custom per-request tracing (trace-id + nvtx ranges), and Flamegraphs from LTTng conversion.
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency per-tenant, batch size distribution, request age at flush, GPU occupancy, kernel launch rate, PCIe bandwidth, scheduler mutex contention (contention histograms), and fairness ratio (slowdown compared to baseline per-tenant).
- Traffic generator: mixture of synthesis and replay. Synthesis workloads: chatty (1-3 tokens per request at 40 rps), bursty enterprise (200-token requests at 10 rps), mixed fanout (100 small tenants, 5 heavy tenants). Replay: production trace snippet (anon) from 2025-01-19 spike.

Experiment matrix (abridged):
- A: baseline slabbed allocator (current prod config).
- B: slabless greedy (no soft-priority).
- C: slabless + age-weighting flush (favor older requests by multiplier).
- D: slabless + tenant-cap admission (simple per-tenant max inflight).
- Variables swept: flush_timeout in {6ms,12ms,24ms,48ms}, max_batch_bytes in {64K,128K,256K}, priority_demotion threshold in {none, 8ms, 16ms}.

Key observations (summary):
- Small-chatty workload (40 rps of 1-3 token requests):
  * Baseline (A): p50=9ms, p95=37ms, p99=92ms, avg_batch_size=1.9
  * Slabless greedy (B): p50=6.2ms (-31%), p95=24ms (-35%), p99=62ms (-33%), avg_batch_size=3.7
  * Slabless+age (C): p50=6.9ms, p95=21ms (best), p99=58ms (best)
  Interpretation: slabless wins here due to coalescing across slabs; age-weighting avoids starvation of earlier requests and improves p95/p99.

- Mixed heavy + many small tenants (stress):
  * Baseline (A): heavy tenants stable, small tenants high tail due to slab fragmentation: heavy p99=78ms, small-tenant p99=124ms
  * Slabless greedy (B): heavy tenant p99 regressed to 142ms (priority inversion), small-tenant p99 improved to 85ms
  * Slabless+tenant-cap (D): heavy p99 back to 82ms, small p99 92ms (compromise)
  Interpretation: slabless without admission control allows small requests to preempt or accumulate in ways that throttle large tenant batches. Enforcing soft per-tenant caps or explicit demotion fixes heavy-tenant regressions.

- GPU utilization and kernel patterns:
  * Slabless increased instantaneous kernel launch rate by ~1.6x when timeout low (6ms). This increased NVTX region churn and slightly higher CPU scheduler contention.
  * Average GPU occupancy rose by 7% for small-chatty runs (good), but variance (stddev) rose for mixed runs, causing occasional stalls observed on A10 nodes.
  * PCIe bandwidth modestly higher due to more frequent small transfers; not saturating but higher overhead per token.

- Contention & mutexes:
  * eBPF stack traces point to increased contention on global batch-queue lock in slabless greedy under high tenant counts.
  * Switching to sharded queue lock (per-tenant or per-priority-bucket) reduced contention 3x in microbench. (See linked PR).

- Tail artifacts and microtraces:
  * p99 spikes often correlated with: KV-cache miss bursts (cache refill stall), concurrent large-batch kernel launches from heavy tenants, and scheduler lock hold time > 2ms during coalescing.
  * Flamegraphs show more time in serialization code paths when batch counts increased rapidly; need to bypass high-overhead serializers for small requests (fast-path).

Representative trace snippets (human readable):
- Trace 1 (small-chatty): 0.1ms request enqueue -> 3.8ms coalesce wait -> 1.2ms serialization -> 0.7ms nvtx kernel -> 0.2ms post-process => total ~6.2ms
- Trace 2 (mixed stress, slabless): request enq 0.9ms -> coalesce wait 14ms -> lock wait 4.6ms -> kernel wait queued -> kernel 9ms -> finish -> total 28.5ms (heavy tenant interleaving)

Conclusions / actionable recommendations:
1) Slabless batching is promising for chatty, low-token workloads; age-weighted flush policy (C) gives the best p95/p99 for those cases. Recommend a feature-flag rollout targeting hosted API small-request routes.
2) For mixed-tenant production traffic, slabless must be paired with tenant-aware admission control or soft caps to protect heavy tenants. The tenant-cap variant (D) is a practical compromise.
3) Implement per-priority-bucket sharded queue locks and a fast-path serializer for small requests to eliminate observed CPU serialization stalls. This significantly reduces mutex contention.
4) Tune timeout distribution adaptively: low baseline timeout (6-12ms) for chatty-only clusters; for mixed clusters, use a biased timeout that increases with cluster load and heavy-tenant presence.
5) Add tracing probes to expose per-tenant cache miss bursts and surface those in Console as a potential root cause when p99 worsens.

Next technical tasks / short-term roadmap (owners):
- PR: sharded-queue-lock + fast-path serializer (owner: Daniel Park) — bench + microtrace (due 2025-03-25).
- PR: slabless feature-flag + age-weighting default (owner: Aisha Kapoor) — AB test on hosted small-route (due 2025-04-02).
- Experiment: tenant-cap policy sweep (D) across cluster sizes (owner: Kenji Sato) — report 2025-04-08.
- Monitoring: add per-tenant KV miss metric and tenant fairness dashboard (product: console team) — request submitted (JIRA:RI-2547).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How does slabless interact with KV-cache prefix caching at larger sequence lengths (>=1024 tokens)? Need separate long-request test.
- Does quantization-induced kernel variance amplify slabless variance? Run on INT8-quantized models.
- Can we implement cheap tenant sampling to detect and preempt priority inversion without strong caps?

Notes-to-self / rough TODOs:
- Capture more nsys profiles for A100 runs (not just A10).
- Re-run mixed-heavy experiments with bigger heavy-tenant cohort (10 heavy tenants) to validate scale.
- Draft short internal one-pager for platform team before any prod rollout.

References / links:
- PR with sharded queue prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runner/pull/842
- Slack discussion summarizing p99 regressions: slack://channel/serving-runtime/thread/1708149123
- JIRA: RI-2476 (slabless experiment epic) and RI-2547 (monitoring items)

Appendix: quick numeric table (selected cells)
- small-chatty (40 rps): A(p99)=92ms | B(p99)=62ms | C(p99)=58ms
- mixed stress: A(heavy-p99)=78ms small-p99=124ms | B(heavy-p99)=142ms small-p99=85ms | D(heavy-p99)=82ms small-p99=92ms

End of journal entry.

-- Aisha K.
